title: Goodwill
hookLine: the intention of non-ill-will: metta as a steering wheel

cards: In the city of Savatthi, the Buddha says, there lived a lady of the house named Vedehika, and everyone said so: so gentle, so calm, so peaceful.
Her maid, Kali, wondered whether that was true, or whether Vedehika had simply never been given a reason to be otherwise. So Kali tested her. One morning she got up late.
Vedehika scowled. The next morning, later still: sharp words. The third morning Kali slept in again, and her well known for it, gentle mistress grabbed a rolling pin and hit her on the head.
Kali ran out bleeding and told the whole street.

teach.b: The Buddha tells that story in the sutta of the simile of the saw, and his point is sharp: a person is gentle only until disagreeable words reach them. Being calm when nobody pushes doesn't prove much.
That's why the second right intention is goodwill.
In Pali it's abyāpāda, literally non-ill-will, and the suttas fill it in with mettā, loving-kindness. Not a warm feeling that washes over you when it likes. An intention: a direction you set.
Think of a steering wheel. The road throws things at you: a rude email, a driver who cuts in, a relative who says the thing. You don't control the road.
You do have your hands on the wheel, and goodwill is which way you turn it. The same sutta then goes about as far as a teaching can go.
Even if bandits were to cut you limb from limb with a two-handled saw, the Buddha says, anyone whose mind filled with hate would not be carrying out his teaching.

He tells the monks to train so their minds stay unshaken, they speak no evil words, and they stay with goodwill toward that very person, and from there toward the whole world. Most of us will never meet those bandits.
We'll meet the slow line at the pharmacy and the group chat. That may be why the same sutta opens with Vedehika and closes with the saw.
The test usually comes in small, ordinary pushes, and each one is a turn of the wheel.

how: Buddhists across traditions practice mettā, often by repeating short phrases of goodwill toward themselves, loved ones, strangers and difficult people; many monastics recite the simile of the saw as a reminder of patience.

o: a warm mood that comes over you on its own
a direction you set, wishing others well
a reputation for being nice to everyone

games.q: who's who in the simile of the saw: tap the pairs.
p: gentle, until her maid tested her

s: goodwill, as right intention, is a warm feeling you wait for
it's an intention, a direction you set: abyāpāda, non-ill-will.
in the simile of the saw, goodwill is meant to hold even toward attackers
MN 21 says a mind filled with hate even then isn't carrying out the teaching.
Vedehika was known for her short temper
she was well-known for being gentle, until her maid tested her.

games.q: you're Vedehika, well-known for your calm. your maid has slept in for the third morning running. what does the story say you did?
o: struck her with a rolling pin.
games.why: in MN 21 the well known for it, gentle Vedehika hit Kali on the head; the Buddha's point is that gentleness shows only when someone pushes.

practice: Think of a conversation you'll probably have today with a little friction in it, and picture the moment where it usually goes sideways.
Rest your hands lightly, as if on a wheel, and set the direction before it begins: whatever they say, turn toward their good, not agreeing with everything, just the direction.
If the old irritation shows up in the picture, notice it, and turn the wheel gently back.

wordCard.voice: Goodwill. Abyāpāda, non-ill-will, the second kind of right intention: not a mood but a direction you set, close kin to mettā.

orig.note: Pali abyāpāda: non-ill-will, the second of the three right intentions, filled in by the suttas with mettā.

carryVoice: Your line: steer by goodwill. You can't control the road, only the wheel. Three hundred sixty-three days, and counting.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 21 (Kakacupama Sutta, the simile of the saw)
Samyutta Nikaya 45.8 (Vibhanga Sutta, the path factors defined)
